client: I've been really stressed out about something happening at work lately, and honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything. There's this colleague of mine, Jessica, and she keeps presenting my ideas in meetings like they're her own, and our manager doesn't seem to notice or care. It's making me feel invisible, like my job could be on the line if I can't even get credit for the work I'm actually doing.
therapist: What you're describing sounds genuinely painful — having your contributions go unrecognized can feel deeply undermining, and I notice that even as you're sharing something so frustrating, there's a quiet heaviness in the way you're expressing it, like you're carrying a lot of this alone. That thought that "talking won't change anything" is worth gently examining together, because it might be your mind protecting you from disappointment, rather than an accurate prediction of what's possible. Let's start by looking at what's actually within your control here — your voice, your documentation, your relationships at work — because you may have more agency in this situation than it feels like right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess you're right that I'm carrying it alone, because I haven't really told anyone about it — not even my friends outside of work. But when you say I have agency, I don't know, it just feels like if I speak up or try to document things, Jessica will find out and make things even worse for me, or my manager will think I'm just being petty and difficult. It's like no matter which way I look at it, doing something feels just as risky as doing nothing.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quietly and quickly, like the words are almost too heavy to say out loud — tells me this fear is very real and very present for you right now, and I want to acknowledge that before anything else. What you're describing is a thinking pattern called "all-or-nothing" — where every path forward looks equally dangerous, which can leave us feeling completely frozen and powerless. But I'd gently invite you to ask: is it possible your mind is predicting the *worst* outcome of speaking up, rather than the *most likely* one?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: Maybe, but the thing is, it's not like I'm imagining something totally out of nowhere — things like this have actually gone badly for me before when I've spoken up at other jobs. So it's hard for me to just tell myself "the worst won't happen" when I have real memories of it actually happening. I hear what you're saying about all-or-nothing thinking, but I'm not sure my fear is completely irrational here.
therapist: You're absolutely right to push back on that, and I want to be clear — your fear *isn't* irrational, it's rooted in real experience, and that deserves to be taken seriously rather than talked away. What I'm hearing, though, is that your past experiences are understandably casting a long shadow over this situation, and it's worth gently exploring whether *this* workplace, *this* manager, and *this* moment are truly the same as those earlier ones — or whether your mind, trying to protect you, might be applying an old map to a new territory. The goal isn't to convince yourself nothing bad could happen, but to make a clearer-eyed choice rather than one driven entirely by fear.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That framing actually helps a little — the idea of an old map on new territory. But when I try to honestly compare this job to the old ones, I realize I don't actually know my manager well enough to predict how he'd react, and that uncertainty feels almost as scary as assuming the worst. It's like I've kept such a low profile trying to stay safe that I've accidentally made myself even more invisible, and now I don't really know what kind of ground I'm standing on.
therapist: There's something really significant in what you just uncovered — that the very strategy you've been using to feel safe has actually deepened the problem, and I can hear in your voice a kind of quiet, tentative recognition of that, like you're carefully stepping onto uncertain ground even as you say it. That insight takes courage, and it's actually a really important starting point — because "I don't know how my manager would react" is not the same as "it will go badly," it's simply *unknown*, and unknown can be worked with. One small, low-risk step might be finding a way to build a little more visibility with your manager that isn't about confronting Jessica at all — just gently starting to map the territory before you decide what to do next.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I like the idea of it not being about confronting Jessica directly, that does feel less terrifying. But I'm struggling to picture what "building visibility" would actually look like in practice — like, do I just start talking more in meetings, or email my manager updates on what I'm working on? It feels a bit forced or transparent, like he might notice I'm suddenly trying harder and wonder what's behind it.
therapist: The way you're speaking — with that careful, almost tentative quality — tells me you're genuinely trying to think this through rather than just dismiss it, which is really encouraging. It's worth noticing that the thought "he'll see through me and judge me for trying" is another prediction your mind is offering as fact — in reality, managers very rarely think "why is this person suddenly contributing?", they mostly just notice the contribution itself. Starting small and naturally, like briefly summarizing your work in an existing one-on-one or asking your manager a thoughtful question about a project, tends to feel less like a performance and more like just... showing up as yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That reframe helps a little — "showing up as yourself" sounds less calculated than "building visibility." But I realize part of the problem is I'm not even sure who I am at this job anymore, because I've been so quiet and careful for so long that I've kind of lost track of what showing up naturally even looks like for me. It's a bit of a lonely feeling, honestly, like I've been fading out without really noticing it until now.
therapist: What you just said — that you've been fading out without noticing — is one of the most honest and tender things you've shared today, and the quiet, reflective way you're saying it tells me this realization is landing somewhere deep and real for you. That sense of losing yourself in the effort to stay safe is actually a really important thing to grieve and acknowledge, not just problem-solve around. And I want to gently offer that this conversation itself — you noticing, naming it, and feeling it — is already a small act of showing up as yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That's... actually a bit hard to hear, in a good way, if that makes sense. I didn't expect to feel emotional about this but there's something about you saying it's okay to grieve it, not just fix it, that makes me feel less like I'm failing at solving a problem. I think I've been so focused on the Jessica situation as something to strategize around that I didn't let myself just feel how much it's worn me down.
therapist: The way your voice carries both tenderness and a kind of quiet relief right now tells me something genuinely important just shifted for you, and I want to stay with that for a moment rather than move past it. What you're describing — exhaustion that's been dressed up as a problem to solve — is something so many people never let themselves acknowledge, and the fact that you're letting yourself feel it now isn't weakness, it's actually the beginning of coming back to yourself. The Jessica situation will still be there to navigate, but you deserve to carry it with a little more self-compassion than you've been allowing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Self-compassion is something I've always kind of rolled my eyes at, honestly — it always sounded like a nice idea that doesn't actually do anything. But sitting here right now, I think I understand it a little differently, like it's less about telling yourself nice things and more about just... not treating your own exhaustion as a character flaw. I'm not sure I know how to actually do that consistently, but I think I want to try.
therapist: The way you just redefined self-compassion — not as positive self-talk, but as simply not weaponizing your own exhaustion against yourself — is genuinely profound, and I think you arrived at that understanding yourself, which makes it far more likely to stick than anything I could have handed you. There's something in your voice right now that sounds both fragile and open, like a door that's been closed for a long time has just been nudged ajar, and I want to honor that. "I want to try" is not a small thing — it's actually exactly where change begins.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Thank you for saying that, though part of me is already wondering if I'll walk out of here and just slip back into the same patterns by tomorrow morning. It's one thing to feel this clarity right now in this room, but the moment Jessica does something in the next meeting, I'm worried all of this will just collapse and I'll be back to feeling invisible and stuck. How do I hold onto this when the situation itself hasn't actually changed yet?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — softly but quickly, like you're trying to hold onto something you're afraid is already slipping — tells me this fear of losing the clarity is real and immediate, and that's actually a very normal part of the change process rather than a sign it won't work. What you're describing isn't a flaw in you, it's just how insight works — it doesn't immunize us against hard moments, it gives us something to return to *after* we've been pulled back in. So the goal isn't to keep this feeling intact forever, it's to remember, when Jessica does something in the next meeting and you feel invisible again, that you've already proven today that you can find your way back to yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That idea of "finding my way back" rather than never losing the thread — that actually feels more manageable than what I was picturing. I think I was putting pressure on myself to somehow stay permanently changed after one session, which is probably its own kind of all-or-nothing thinking when I say it out loud. I'm still scared it'll be harder than it sounds in the moment, but I think I can at least try to remember that today happened.
therapist: You just caught yourself in real time — noticing that expecting permanent change from one session is its own all-or-nothing thinking — and that *is* the skill, that's exactly what finding your way back looks like in practice. I notice there's still something a little fragile and uncertain in the way you're holding all of this, like you're speaking quietly around something precious you don't want to drop, and that's okay — you don't have to feel certain for this to be real. What happened today happened, and "I can try to remember that" is enough to start with.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
